title: How Much Concrete for an 8x10 Shed Slab? 4-Inch Example
description: An 8x10 shed slab poured 4 inches thick needs 0.99 cu yd of concrete, or 45 bags of 80 lb mix. See how the count works and when to compare ready-mix.

sources.title: Quikrete Concrete Mix No. 1101 data sheet

body.text: A shed slab 10 feet long, 8 feet wide and 4 inches thick needs 0.99 cu yd of concrete, which works out to 45 bags of 80 lb mix with no extra added for spillage. Your pad may be a different size, so enter your own measurements into the [Concrete Calculator](/concrete-calculator) before you buy.
The worked example

This example uses a slab 10 feet long, 8 feet wide and 4 inches thick. Measure the pad you plan to pour, since its size may not match the shed's outside dimensions. A slab that extends past the shed walls or is smaller than the footprint will change the result, so use the pad's own measurements.
How the volume is calculated
The calculator works through the same steps you would use with a pencil. Here is how each step applies to this slab.

items: Multiply length by width to get the area, then multiply that area by the thickness in inches. Divide the result by 12 to convert inches to feet. The answer is cubic feet of concrete. For this slab, the volume is 26.67 cu ft.
Divide the cubic feet by 27 to get cubic yards. For this slab, the volume is 0.99 cu yd.
Divide the cubic feet by the yield of one bag. An 80 lb bag yields 0.6 cu ft, so the exact count is 44.4 bags.
Round up to whole bags. The result is 45 bags.

body.text: Why the bag count is 45

The exact count is 44.4 bags, but you cannot buy part of a bag, so the calculator rounds up to 45 bags. Rounding up means you have enough material to finish the pour, so you do not run short partway through.

The 0.6 cubic foot yield is the figure used for an 80 lb bag in the calculator. Products differ, so check the cubic feet per bag printed on the label of the bag you actually buy. If the label shows a different yield, divide the 26.67 cu ft by that number instead and round up.
When to compare ready-mix delivery
At 0.99 cu yd, you are close to one full cubic yard. That is the point where it is worth asking a ready-mix supplier for a quote and comparing it with buying 45 bags.

Whether a truck makes sense depends on your local supplier's minimum order, delivery fees and how far you are from the plant. Some suppliers may not deliver a load this small at all, so ask before you plan around it.

Each bag weighs 80 pounds, so 45 bags means a lot of hauling, mixing and placing by hand. Weigh that physical work against the delivery cost, and consider whether you have the help and time to mix and place the full amount in one session.
Adding extra for spillage

This example uses 0 percent extra. If you expect spills, uneven ground or a rough edge, the calculator lets you add an allowance before it rounds up. Rerun the calculator with your own percentage to see the new bag count. The extra amount changes the volume before the bags are counted, so the bag count can rise.
Pitfalls to avoid

items: Measuring the shed instead of the slab. The pad may be larger or smaller than the shed's outside dimensions.
Mixing up units. Length and width go in feet, and thickness goes in inches.
Treating 4 inches as 4 feet. Thickness must be entered in inches, or the volume will be far too large.
Buying bags by weight alone. Check the cubic feet per bag on the label, because products differ.
Forgetting to round up. A result of 44.4 bags means you need 45 bags, not 44.

body.text: Plan the pour

Confirm your dimensions, thickness and bag count before you order or mix. Keep the bag label handy so you can check the yield on the exact product you buy. For other sizes and bag types, see [how many bags of concrete for a 10x10 slab](/blog/how-many-bags-of-concrete-for-10x10-slab) and [how many yards of concrete for a 20x20 patio](/blog/how-many-yards-of-concrete-for-20x20-patio). If you are weighing gravel under the slab, the [how much gravel for a shed base](/blog/how-much-gravel-for-shed-base-12x12) post shows a similar calculation in tons.
FAQ
Can I use this count for a shed slab of a different size?

No. The steps work for any length, width and thickness, but the numbers in this example only apply to a 10 by 8 foot slab, 4 inches thick. Enter your own measurements into the [Concrete Calculator](/concrete-calculator) to get your count.
Why does the calculator round up to whole bags?
Concrete mix is sold in whole bags, so a fractional bag does not help you finish the pour. Rounding up gives you enough material to complete the slab.
Does the calculator replace the product label?
No. Always check the coverage or yield printed on the product label, because products differ. Use the calculator with your own measurements, then confirm the cubic feet per bag on the bag you buy.
